Heard on admission.
Admitted.

This criminal appeal under Section 372(2) of Cr.P.C. has been preferred to challenge the order dated 18.03.2024 passed by the Special Judge (Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988) Bhopal (M.P.) in MJCR No.1963/2022, whereunder the closure report filed by respondent N o.1 (conveniently referred to as EOW) was allowed, and investigation in Crime No.14/2019 of EOW instituted against respondents No.2 to 20 was dropped.
2. sentences.text: 3. The said committee submitted its report on 07.03.2019 upon which FIR of Crime No.14/2019 was registered in Bhopal Unit of EOW regarding offence of Sections 409, 420 and 120B IPC and Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
The matter was investigated and finally a closure report bearing No.11/2020 was submitted before the concerned Court.
Vide its order dated 11.04.2022 the Court rejected the closure report and directed to further investigate the points highlighted in the order.

The matter was again taken up for investigation and this time also no evidence was found regarding the commission of crime, therefore, a closure report was again submitted before the Special Court which was accepted under the impugned order.

4. In this criminal appeal the grounds taken are that the impugned order is perverse as it has purposely ignored the enquiry committee report dated 18.01.2019, having details about several irregularities committed by Brijkishore Kuthiala during his Chancellorship from 2003-2018; he was instrumental in giving undue advantage and illegal appointment to respondents No.3 to 20;
respondent No.2 with dishonest intention provided financial profits to his well wishers and also facilitated the appointments contrary to UGC norms.

Further, the second closure report dated 01.11.2022 was filed without supplying any copy to the appellant, inspite the fact that NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:1072 3 CRA-10612-2024 while appellant was examined as witness No.3, while considering the first closure report.

The learned Special Court, under the impugned order, allowed the closure report and permitted the investigation to be dropped, but said order is violative of legal propositions, hence, deserves to be quashed.
A request is therefore made to allow the appeal and direct the respondent No.1 to file the charge-sheet and also to direct the trial Court to decide the case on merits.

5. Learned counsel for the respondent No.1 has challenged this criminal appeal on the ground that in legal framework, a criminal appeal would not lie against the impugned order, particularly under Section of 372(2) of Cr.P.C read with Section 413 of BNSS, 2023.
It has also been argued that appellant has no locus to challenge the impugned order as he was not the informant in this case.
6. We have heard the learned counsel for both the sides, and have perused the record as well as relevant provisions of law.
7. From the order under challenge, it is evident that the Court below while deciding MJCR No.1963/2022, did not pass any order of acquittal in favour of respondents No.2-20.
It merely accepted the closure report filed under Section 173(2)(ii) of Cr.P.C.
Dropping the proceeding at a stage, where even the charge-sheet is not filed before the concerned Court, can never be given the color of acquittal.

Section 372 of Cr.P.C, 1973 and also Section 413 of BNSS, 2023 allow the victim to prefer an appeal only against an order of acquittal or an order convicting for a lesser offence/imposing inadequate compensation.

None of these conditions are prevailing here, therefore the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:1072 4 CRA-10612-2024 objection of learned counsel for the respondent No.1 regarding maintainability of this proceeding under Section 372(2)

sentences.text: 8. The other objection raised herein by respondent No.1 is that the appellant was not a party before the Special Court nor was he the first informant in the case, therefore he has no locus to challenge the impugned order.

Section 173(2)(ii) of Cr.P.C. has a mandate that before allowing a closure report filed under Section 173 of Cr.P.C, 1973, the person, if any, by whom the information relating to the commission of offence was first given, should be served with a notice.

Here the appellant,
admittedly, does not carry the status of first informant.

It seems that after the registration of FIR,
his statements were recorded by the concerned police officer and during consideration of first closure report, the Special Court summoned him as witness and recorded his statement as witness No.4.
These proceedings by themselves do not confer the status of first informant upon the appellant.

9. In the case of Bhagwat Singh vs. Commissioner of Police and anr. AIR 1985 SC 1285, the Apex Court observed that when on a basis of Police report, Magistrate prefers to drop the proceedings,
instead of taking cognizance of offence, the first informant has a right to be heard at the time of consideration of report by the Magistrate and to protect this right, a notice needs to be issued to him.

entities.text: Bhagwat Singh vs. Commissioner of Police and anr. AIR 1985 SC 1285
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Apex Court also deliberated on the question of obligation of Magistrate to issue notice to the injured person or to the relative of deceased for providing him an opportunity to be heard and opined NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:1072 5 CRA-10612-2024 that no such obligation can be fixed upon the Magistrate, but clarified that if any person having that status appears before the Magistrate, he needs to be heard.
10. The case in hand shows that Special Court had rightly not issued any notice to the appellant while considering the second closure report and passing the impugned order.

Further, the appellant did not join the proceeding on his own and file any protest petition in Special Court to challenge the closure report, therefore, being a stranger to that proceeding and having no direct interest in the litigation under question, the appellant has no locus to be heard in this appeal against the impugned order.
11. Consequently, this appeal fails on the ground of maintainability and also for the reason that appellant has no locus to challenge the impugned order.
Appeal is therefore dismissed.
(SUSHRUT ARVIND DHARMADHIKARI) (ANURADHA   JUDGE JUDG
